title: MLOps: From Experiments to Reliable AI Systems
text:
Contents
An AI model becomes a reliable product only when the underlying infrastructure makes execution reproducible, observable, and resilient to failure. This book develops the platform engineering foundations of enterprise MLOps: distributed cluster training, predictable high-throughput serving, telemetry and evaluation gates, reliable storage and retrieval state, and automated workflow orchestration. It connects individual engineering decisions into a continuous, self-improving production lifecycle.

title: MLOps: From Experiments to Reliable AI Systems
text:
Front matter

Introduction: the operating problem
A model can be impressive in an isolated experiment and still fail as a product. Production introduces traffic, failures, shared resources, changing data, delayed ground truth, cost limits, deployment risk, and a reproducibility requirement. Together, these constraints turn a one-time model result into a system whose behavior, state, and changes can be explained.



Part I: Reproducible training at cluster scale
A training run must preserve identified inputs and recovery evidence when model state or execution time requires several GPUs or machines.

Making ML runs reproducible
Which information and responsibilities make training or serving repeatable? The introduction established that production adds shared resources, failure, and evidence requirements. The artifacts, responsibility split, and infrastructure choices together turn an ad-hoc run into a repeatable system.
Distributed training across devices and clusters
How can one training job use many GPUs without turning communication, scheduling, or failure into the real bottleneck? Chapter 1 defined the versioned artifacts and software layers around a run. Single-GPU limits lead to network and process identities, then to recoverable distributed execution and measurement.



Part II: Reliable model services with measurement and retrieval
A trained model still needs a service that can handle requests within time and memory limits. A fast response alone does not show that its answer is correct. Applications that answer from external documents also depend on reliable storage and relevant retrieved evidence.

Serving LLMs with predictable performance
How does a versioned model become a responsive, efficient, and reversible user-facing service? Chapter 2 treated one coordinated training job whose ranks progress together. Serving replaces synchronized steps with variable-length requests, latency objectives, retained KV-cache state, and rolling changes across a fleet.
Measuring service health and model quality
How can operators distinguish an available service from a useful and trustworthy AI system? Chapter 3 produced a serving bundle with performance and quality gates. Infrastructure telemetry, drift signals, AI traces, experiments, repeated evaluator runs, and production feedback provide the evidence.
Keeping storage and retrieval state reliable
Which storage system fits each artifact, and how does retrieval state remain correct as data and embeddings change? Earlier chapters produced checkpoints, while Chapter 4 added traces, evaluation cases, and experiment records that outlive individual processes. Access patterns lead to storage semantics and then to a versioned vector-retrieval system with reproducible derived indexes.



Part III: Automated workflows and reliable system operation
Independent inference endpoints, storage databases, and training jobs become brittle and unmaintainable without automated dependency scheduling, idempotent retry policies, and coordinated incident remediation across components.

Running repeatable ML workflows
How can the system reproduce a multi-step ML result after partial failure, schedule delay, code change, or operator handoff? Chapter 5 established durable artifacts and rebuildable derived state. Dependency graphs replace manual command sequences with tasks that have explicit inputs, outputs, resources, retries, and evidence.
Operating a grounded-answer system end to end
How do all six layers cooperate when a production answer becomes less grounded even though the service remains available? The preceding chapters produced versioned artifacts, recoverable distributed jobs, serving bundles, evidence, durable and derived storage, and retryable pipelines. Those results form one system whose release records connect an alert to a verified recovery.



Appendices

Formula reference
A quantitative result is meaningful only when its workload, aggregation window, and version context are known. The relationships cover cost, capacity, memory, synchronization, latency, evaluation, storage, retrieval, and pipeline duration. Their values support comparison and diagnosis while the surrounding evidence explains each production decision.
MLOps glossary
MLOps combines vocabulary from infrastructure, distributed systems, model evaluation, storage, retrieval, and orchestration. The same term can connect several components, so each definition names the object, behavior, or measurement involved. The entries use consistent meanings across training, serving, evaluation, storage, and pipelines.
Questions and concise answers
A production failure can cross artifacts, compute, serving, evidence, storage, retrieval, and orchestration. The questions trace those connections through one system and one quality incident. The answers identify the responsible component, evidence, failure cause, and recovery path.

title: Introduction: the operating problem
text:
Scope boundaries
A model can be impressive in an isolated experiment and still fail as a product. Production introduces traffic, failures, shared resources, changing data, delayed ground truth, cost limits, deployment risk, and a reproducibility requirement. Together, these constraints turn a one-time model result into a system whose behavior, state, and changes can be explained.
Machine learning operations, or MLOps, connects model development to the systems that run, measure, and maintain it. This book develops that platform: the compute, serving software, measurements, storage, and scheduled work needed to keep a model service useful as demand and data change. The starting knowledge is basic Python functions and loops, files and processes, and arithmetic with rates and percentages. A GPU is a processor that can perform many numerical operations in parallel. A tensor is an array of numbers, such as a vector or matrix, that model software processes on a CPU or GPU.
A reliable machine learning system begins with saved inputs and software that make a run reproducible. It then scales computation, serves a large language model (LLM) under time and memory constraints, measures service and model behavior, stores lasting state, and connects the work into pipelines. A question-answering service that uses retrieved source material connects this complete loop. The book follows three stages. Part I establishes reproducible training at cluster scale. Part II develops reliable model services with measurement and retrieval. Part III connects automated workflows to reliable system operation.
A model’s numerical parameters, often called weights, determine how it transforms an input into a prediction. Three operating modes use these same parameters differently. The distinction matters because it changes what must be stored, measured, and recovered.
A small numerical example makes the state changes visible. Suppose an illustrative one-parameter model predicts normalized compute demand by multiplying one numeric workload input by one weight. Input and demand are dimensionless multiples of chosen baseline values. The following values are illustrative, not production measurements. The training example has input 2 and target 1, and the initial weight is 0.2.
This trace is the smallest version of the operating loop. Training produces changed model state, evaluation produces evidence for a release decision, and inference produces outputs and service measurements. A saved training state is a checkpoint. A deployable package of the model and its runtime inputs is a serving bundle. Their identities must connect to the input data and software that produced them, which is the problem Chapter 1 develops. The simple optimizer above needs no running statistics, while the Adam optimizer discussed in Chapter 2 keeps additional state. A neural network also retains more intermediate activations than this one-multiply example.
Evaluation can itself use a model. A judge performs inference on a question, generated answer, source evidence, and scoring rule. Those items are its input, and its judgment is the output. The answer-producing model and the judge both keep fixed parameters. To evaluate the judge, its judgment is compared with a separate human reference label. Agreement with that reference measures the judge, not the response time or training loss of the answer-producing model. Chapter 4 develops these distinct measurements.
The focus is the platform around model work: allocating compute, coordinating training, serving requests, measuring behavior, preserving data, and automating repeatable work. Low-level GPU kernel authoring, proprietary hardware compilation, and model architecture design are outside this scope. Product names identify examples of component roles, not requirements to use a particular provider. Packaging can fix the application libraries and runtime files without fixing the host machine’s GPU driver. The required compatibility remains a separate condition, explained in Section 1.4.
Several terms connect the stages below. In distributed training, a rank is one process’s integer identity within a cooperating group, and world size is the number of processes in that group. Local rank identifies the process within its node, commonly to choose a GPU. These identities let the software direct communication to the right participants. Section 2.5 explains how the group is formed.
For language-model inference, prefill processes the prompt tokens, and decode generates successive output tokens. The key-value (KV) cache stores numerical attention state from earlier tokens so the engine can reuse that state during generation. It is request-related working state, not a parameter update. Sections 3.3 and 3.5 connect these phases to time and memory costs. To locate that time across software components, a span records one timed operation, such as retrieval. A child span identifies the operation that called it, its parent. Connected spans form a request trace, developed in Section 4.1.
Some training systems learn from rewards for actions rather than a supplied target for each prediction. In this reinforcement learning setup, an actor runs the current model to choose actions and collects a trajectory, the sequence of observations, actions, and rewards. Reward is the numerical feedback used by the training objective, and rollout length counts the steps collected. A learner consumes these records, calculates an objective, and updates model parameters. Actor collection and learner updates have different throughput measurements. This distinction supplies the context for the workflow measurements in Section 6.9.

1.1 Coordinating ML development and operations
Which information and responsibilities make training or serving repeatable? The introduction established that production adds shared resources, failure, and evidence requirements. The artifacts, responsibility split, and infrastructure choices together turn an ad-hoc run into a repeatable system.
Reproducing a result starts with identifying the inputs and the software that used them. The deployment platform must then provide a compatible environment and enough capacity. The map connects these decisions to the handoff between the people who develop a model and those who operate its service.
One experimental run proves that code can run once. The unresolved problem is making the same intent repeatable for other people, machines, and dates. The lifecycle and the engineering disciplines around it provide the starting point.
MLOps does not replace machine learning research. It creates a controlled path around research. Inputs are identifiable, compute is requested explicitly, outputs are stored with lineage, deployments are reversible, and production evidence can become the next evaluation or training case.
Four disciplines contribute different guarantees to that path:

Machine Learning Operations (MLOps): The combined engineering practice for automating, operating, measuring, and scaling training, inference, and data pipelines. The glossary collects the terms used across these activities.




Machine learning: defines the model, objective, data meaning, and quality measurements.
Software engineering: turns experimental logic into testable packages, APIs, and maintainable interfaces.
Data engineering: moves, validates, transforms, and retains the records that training and evaluation consume.
DevOps and platform engineering: provisions compute, deploys services, isolates tenants, observes failures, and automates recovery.


System principle
Operational reproducibility requires identifiable software and data dependencies:

The production unit is more than a weight file. It is a versioned bundle of code, data definitions, model artifacts, runtime configuration, infrastructure assumptions, and evaluation evidence.
If one ingredient changes without a new identity, the team cannot reliably restore the earlier configuration. Matching inputs makes comparison possible, but does not by itself guarantee identical numerical outputs on every hardware and software combination.

1.2 Tracking artifacts and their dependencies
The MLOps mission now has four contributing disciplines. Coordination still fails when their outputs live as unnamed local files or remembered commands. Explicit artifact types and immutable input-output links make every transformation traceable.

Artifact: A stored, addressable output whose identity links directly to the code, configuration, and inputs that produced it.

A minimal artifact chain links seven stored results or input descriptions:

The source revision identifies executable logic through a Git commit hash or a locked source archive.
The environment identifies application libraries and runtime files. A container image digest fixes the image contents, including packaged Python dependencies, CUDA userspace libraries, and framework versions. The host GPU driver remains separate and must satisfy the recorded compatibility requirements.
The dataset snapshot identifies the records, schema checks, and training or evaluation split definitions.
The run configuration records hyperparameters, random seeds, and compute requests. The software consumes this configuration and the dataset within the selected environment.
The checkpoint saves model parameters and the state needed to resume training, such as optimizer buffers and the completed step.
The evaluation record connects a checkpoint to its cases, predictions, reference values, and measured scores. Evaluation produces evidence without updating those model parameters.
The serving bundle packages the approved weights, tokenizer, runtime settings, and release metadata. Its identity connects the deployed behavior to the evaluation evidence. Section 3.8 develops this release unit.

Lineage is the directed relationship between these objects. A metric points to exact evaluation outputs, the outputs point to model and dataset versions, and a deployment points to the serving bundle that passed its gates. A filename such as model-final-v2.bin carries none of those guarantees.

Troubleshooting walkthrough: reconstructing a failed training run
This incident investigation traces a failed checkpoint through its lineage to restore execution:

Observed symptom: The evaluation task reports a missing checkpoint after the training worker exited.
Identity lookup: The run manifest resolves the source revision, image digest, dataset snapshot, configuration hash, worker attempt, and expected checkpoint generation.
Lineage check: The artifact store contains an attempt-scoped temporary file but no committed completion manifest, so the output is not treated as consumable.
Recovery decision: The pipeline retries from the last complete checkpoint with the same immutable inputs, while the failed attempt and its logs remain attached to the run.
Evidence retained: The final record links the failure, retry, checkpoint generation, evaluator result, and release decision without relying on a remembered command.
Conclusion: A failed process becomes diagnosable when every output has an identity and a publication state.

1.3 Assigning responsibilities across research and platform software
Versioned artifacts make work reproducible. The remaining question is how much infrastructure the team manages directly. Managed services, Kubernetes, virtual machines, and bare metal expose progressively more control and responsibility.

Infrastructure responsibility: The division of infrastructure work between the application team and a platform or cloud provider.
Managed service: A provider-operated platform that exposes a workload interface while the provider runs much of the supporting infrastructure.
Kubernetes: A cluster system that places and restarts containerized workloads on a pool of machines.
Virtual machine: An isolated software-defined computer with its own operating system, running on shared physical hardware.
Bare metal: A physical server assigned directly to the workload without a virtual-machine layer.
Serverless execution: A provider-run execution model in which the team submits code or a container without managing the underlying machines.

Infrastructure choices form a continuum. Serverless execution removes machine management but constrains runtime, networking, accelerators, and customization. Virtual machines and bare metal expose those controls together with patching, scheduling, recovery, and capacity risk.

Infrastructure responsibility: purpose and limits
The division of operational responsibility defines the scope of control across platforms:

Works on: The complete workload.
Helps when: Delivery speed, custom hardware, isolation, and available support skills point to different options.
How it works: Required controls narrow the options. The remaining choice determines which infrastructure work stays with the team.
Other limits: Managed products may lack required multi-step workflows, rich telemetry, networking, or update behavior.
Why it matters: The choice affects both workload capability and the amount of infrastructure work the team carries.

1.4 Reproducible environments with containers
The deployment option determines who manages the host. The application still needs a portable runtime that behaves the same across development and production. Image construction, registry distribution, and container execution are distinct parts of that runtime path.

Container image: An immutable filesystem and metadata template containing application code, libraries, and its startup command.
Container: A running process created from an image and isolated with operating-system mechanisms while sharing the host kernel.
Registry: A service that stores versioned image layers and supplies them to deployment systems.

A Dockerfile turns declared build inputs into image layers. Stable dependency steps usually precede frequently changing source code, which allows cached layers to be reused. Multi-stage builds keep build-only tools out of the runtime image, reducing transfer time and security exposure.
The following abbreviated Dockerfile uses Python 3.12 and uv 0.6.16, a Python dependency manager. Its inputs are a compatible pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and an application in src/. It builds a CPU Python service image whose startup command runs src.service. It does not package a GPU runtime or model weights. A GPU service needs compatible CUDA userspace libraries in its image and an independently installed host driver exposed through the container runtime. The Dockerfile uses version 1 frontend syntax. The Python base tags remain mutable in this compact example, so a reproducible release must replace them with verified image digests and record the target processor architecture.

Code example: A two-stage build produces an immutable runtime image.


# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN pip install uv==0.6.16 && uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/.venv /app/.venv
COPY src/ ./src/
ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH"
CMD ["python", "-m", "src.service"]

Code walkthrough: multi-stage container packaging
The multi-stage build separates dependency resolution from the final runtime image:

Build stage: uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project installs the locked production dependencies into /app/.venv without trying to build application code that has not yet been copied.
Runtime stage: COPY --from=build transfers the resolved environment without transferring the package manager’s build context or compiler tools.
Application layer: COPY src/ appears late, which lets the slower dependency layer remain cached across ordinary source edits.
Startup command: CMD names the module that the deployment starts. The image digest identifies the complete image filesystem and command.
Result: A successful build creates a runtime image with the Python base, installed dependencies, and service files. It does not start the service until a container is launched.
Limits: Missing files or failed dependency installation stop the build. Runtime health checks, a non-root user, vulnerability policy, secret mounts, and automatic recovery are omitted. The application must be importable from /app and any required native runtime libraries must be present in the final stage.


Secrets copied into an image or passed through persistent build arguments remain in layer history. Runtime secret mounts and narrowly scoped workload permissions avoid that exposure. Containers share the host kernel, so untrusted or agent-generated code generally requires a stronger sandbox or a microVM.

Architecture compatibility: hardware target verification
Processor architecture differences can cause runtime failures across build and execution hosts:

A laptop with an ARM processor can build an image that will not run on an x86 cloud node.
An explicit target platform, immutable digest, and a test on the production CPU/GPU runtime family establish compatibility.

1.5 Sizing self-hosted capacity and cost
Containers make a runtime portable across deployment options. A large language model adds expensive accelerators, large weight transfers, and ongoing infrastructure work. The service objective determines the capacity assumptions used to compare hosted APIs with self-hosting.
An open model gives control over weights, architecture, fine-tuning, data placement, and runtime. Self-hosting also makes the team responsible for availability, throughput, scaling, security, weight distribution, and evaluation. The decision is not simply price per token. It compares a provider bill with the full cost of hardware, platform engineering, idle capacity, incidents, and optimization.
Total cost of ownership combines costs over one common period and in one currency. In the expression below, each \(C\) term is a cost: fixed commitments, compute, storage, network, operations, or expected risk. \(V_{\mathrm{residual}}\) is recoverable value at the period’s end, so it is subtracted. The categories must not overlap. Compute already paid for by a reservation is not counted again as usage. Expected risk is an estimate of possible losses, not a guaranteed future bill.
\[
C_{\mathrm{total}} = C_{\mathrm{fixed}} + C_{\mathrm{compute}} + C_{\mathrm{storage}} + C_{\mathrm{network}} + C_{\mathrm{operations}} + C_{\mathrm{risk}} - V_{\mathrm{residual}}
\tag{1.1}\]

Cost allocation example: one-year ownership cost
Evaluating self-hosted infrastructure expenses combines multiple cost components:

Fixed commitment: Reserved hardware and platform commitments cost $120,000.
Usage: Compute, storage, and network usage total $205,000.
Operations: On-call, maintenance, and platform engineering allocate $90,000.
Risk and residual: Expected interruption or shortage exposure is $30,000, while recoverable equipment value is $10,000.
Total: The one-year comparison cost is $120,000 + $205,000 + $90,000 + $30,000 − $10,000 = $435,000.
Conclusion: A fair comparison with an API or managed-service alternative uses the same demand, reliability, and quality assumptions. The formula reference provides the relationship for later lookup.


Replica sizing starts with a measured service rate. \(Q_{\mathrm{peak}}\) is peak demand in requests per second, and \(Q_{\mathrm{replica}}\) is one replica’s sustainable rate at the latency target. The planning fraction \(u\), with \(0 < u \leq 1\), reserves headroom by reducing that measured rate to \(Q_{\mathrm{replica}}u\). Dividing demand by the planned rate gives the number of replicas carrying traffic. The ceiling brackets \(\lceil\ \rceil\) round up because a fraction of a replica cannot be deployed. \(R_{\mathrm{redundancy}}\) adds the spare replicas required by the selected failure scenario, giving the total \(R_{\mathrm{needed}}\).
\[
R_{\mathrm{needed}} = \left\lceil  \frac{Q_{\mathrm{peak}}}{Q_{\mathrm{replica}} \cdot u} \right\rceil + R_{\mathrm{redundancy}}
\tag{1.2}\]

Capacity sizing example: replicas for a 60 request-per-second peak
Calculating required serving instances accounts for throughput headroom and failure reserves:

Measured capacity: One serving replica sustains 8 requests/s while meeting the latency target.
Headroom: At 75% normal utilization, an 8 requests/s benchmark yields 6 planned requests/s per replica.
Demand replicas: A 60 requests/s peak divided by 6 planned requests/s requires 10 replicas.
Failure allowance: Two additional replicas cover maintenance or one failed host group.
Starting deployment: Adding 2 spare replicas to the 10 demand replicas produces a 12-replica starting deployment. A load test with the real prompt and output-length mix checks the estimate.
Conclusion: Capacity is a measured property of a serving bundle, not a value inferred from model parameter count alone.


Model quality, prompt length, output length, quantization, engine version, GPU type, batching, and latency objectives all change per-replica capacity. The estimate assumes compatible replicas and traffic that the router can distribute across them. Two spare replicas cover a host failure only if that failure removes no more than two replicas and the remaining placement can carry the demand. The estimate belongs to one exact serving bundle and failure model. A changed ingredient requires a new capacity measurement.

Handoff record: release criteria checklist
A release handoff makes the decision and recovery path inspectable:

A training team hands over a serving bundle only when the window, accountable owner, escalation path, release identity, rollback target, and evidence links are recorded.
The receiving team can then answer what changed, which checks passed, who can stop the rollout, and which known-good version is restored if a gate fails.

2.1 Accounting for single-GPU memory use
How can one training job use many GPUs without turning communication, scheduling, or failure into the real bottleneck? Chapter 1 defined the versioned artifacts and software layers around a run. Single-GPU limits lead to network and process identities, then to recoverable distributed execution and measurement.
The memory budget determines which training state must be divided across devices. Communication then keeps their updates consistent, while scheduling brings the complete worker group into service. The map follows this progression into checkpoint recovery and measurements of useful work, which determine whether a larger cluster actually improves the run.
A reproducible run can still be physically impossible on one device. The first question is whether model state, optimizer state, and activations fit, followed by whether the run finishes in an acceptable time. The memory objects reveal which parallelism strategies can satisfy the constraint.
The training trace in the introduction distinguished parameters, activations, gradients, and optimizer state. The estimate below counts one full training replica with no model-state sharding or offload. \(P\) is the number of parameters. \(b_w\) and \(b_g\) are bytes stored per weight and gradient, \(b_{\mathrm{master}}\) counts any higher-precision master copy, and \(b_{\mathrm{opt}}\) counts optimizer buffers per parameter. \(A\) is the activation memory retained for the current micro-batch, in bytes. A micro-batch is the subset processed in one forward and backward pass before any optional gradient accumulation.
Multiplying the parameter count by the sum of its storage costs gives the model-state subtotal. Adding \(A\) gives the approximate device memory \(M_{\mathrm{train}}\). Optimizers and precision policies allocate different buffers, so a missing master copy contributes zero rather than an assumed allocation. The estimate excludes temporary communication buffers, kernel workspace, and allocator reserve. The calculation uses decimal GB, where 1 GB is \(10^9\) bytes. BF16 is a 16-bit floating-point format, requiring 2 bytes per value, while FP32 uses 4 bytes. Adam keeps running averages of gradients and squared gradients, its two moment buffers, to adapt parameter updates.
\[
M_{\mathrm{train}} ≈ P\left(b_w + b_g + b_{\mathrm{master}} + b_{\mathrm{opt}}\right) + A
\tag{2.1}\]
The memory figure separates the stored values involved in an update. Its key implication is that fitting the inference weights does not establish that the training state fits.
The second limit is elapsed time. Data parallelism can reduce time by processing more samples or tokens per step, but only while extra computation exceeds the communication and synchronization cost. Model sharding addresses memory, while data replication addresses throughput. Large jobs usually combine both.

Device: One accelerator visible to a training process, such as one NVIDIA GPU.
Server or node: One physical or virtual machine containing CPUs, host memory, storage interfaces, networking, and one or more devices.





Memory breakdown: 8-billion-parameter model with Adam optimizer
Evaluating GPU memory consumption across training components highlights persistent versus transient allocations:

Weights: Eight billion BF16 weights at 2 bytes each require 16 GB.
Gradients: BF16 gradients add 16 GB.
Master weights: Eight billion FP32 master weights at 4 bytes each add 32 GB.
Adam state: Two FP32 moment buffers use 8 bytes per parameter and add 64 GB.
Model-state subtotal: Weights, gradients, master weights, and Adam state occupy 128 GB at the point when these allocations coexist. Gradients may be released between steps, unlike parameters and optimizer state.
Activations: For illustration, 40 GB at a short micro-batch gives about 168 GB total, while 160 GB at a longer sequence or larger micro-batch gives about 288 GB. A profiler or shape-based activation estimate supplies the value for a real run.
Conclusion: An 8B model that is easy to load for inference can require multiple high-memory GPUs for ordinary Adam training.

2.2 Matching communication paths to model traffic
Memory accounting shows why multiple devices are necessary. The devices cannot cooperate until their physical links, communication library, framework API, and parallelism strategy are distinguished. The stack runs from physical links through communication software to the parallelism strategy.
A rank is one process’s integer identity within a cooperating group. World size is the number of processes in that group, and local rank identifies a process within its node, commonly to select its GPU. For two nodes with four processes each, world size is eight. Global ranks are 0 through 7, while each node uses local ranks 0 through 3. A subgroup, such as four processes splitting one matrix operation, can have its own rank numbering and size.
Distributed training uses four different kinds of technology:

Physical fabric: PCIe, NVLink/NVSwitch, InfiniBand, RoCE, or Ethernet moves bytes between devices or nodes.
Communication backend: NCCL implements GPU collectives, operations involving all processes in a group, and selects supported transport paths. Gloo or MPI cover other process and data patterns.
Framework API: torch.distributed creates process groups and exposes collectives to PyTorch code.
Parallelism strategy: Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) replicates the model. Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) divides its stored state. Tensor parallelism splits a layer’s matrix operations, while pipeline parallelism assigns groups of layers to devices. These choices determine what must cross each link.

NVLink is not NCCL: NVLink is a high-bandwidth intra-server fabric, whereas NCCL is a software library that may use NVLink, InfiniBand, RoCE, or sockets. torch.distributed is the PyTorch API that requests collective operations from a backend, not a physical network.



Table 2.1: Fabric scope constrains the placement of communication-heavy parallelism.










Connection type
Typical scope
Why placement matters

Within one server
Tensor-parallel communication can occur every layer and needs very high bandwidth.

Data, pipeline, or context groups exchange gradients, activations, or KV state across nodes.

Functional for rendezvous and small transfers but often too slow for large synchronized tensors.







Device placement example: placing a tensor-parallel group across fast interconnects
Mapping parallel process groups to physical interconnects prevents cross-node communication bottlenecks:

Tensor payload: Four tensor-parallel ranks exchange layer outputs on nearly every transformer layer.
Fast local fabric: One server contains four GPUs connected through NVLink or NVSwitch, so the group remains inside that server.
Across servers: A larger data-parallel group crosses InfiniBand or RoCE only at gradient synchronization points.
Failure signal: If a tensor-parallel rank is placed across ordinary Ethernet, per-layer collective time rises and every downstream stage waits.
Conclusion: Communication frequency and payload size determine which parallel group benefits most from the fastest available link.

text:
2.3 Gradient synchronization in distributed training
The communication stack now has distinct layers. The simplest scaling baseline is a full model replica on each device, with one consistent update shared across replicas. Data sharding, local backpropagation, all-reduce, and optimizer stepping form the update sequence.

Distributed Data Parallel (DDP): A strategy that gives every process a model replica. Each process trains on a distinct batch shard and synchronizes gradients before applying the same optimizer update.

A DDP process owns one model replica and usually one GPU. A DistributedSampler gives each rank a different sample subset. During backpropagation, DDP groups parameter gradients into buckets and launches asynchronous all-reduce operations as soon as a bucket is ready. Overlap hides some communication behind the remaining backward computation.
All-reduce combines corresponding values from every participating rank and returns the combined values to all of them. Let \(N\) be the world size, \(r\) a rank from 0 through \(N-1\), and \(g_r\) that rank’s local gradient vector. Every vector has one component per parameter in the same order. The average \(g_{\mathrm{global}}\) is their sum divided by \(N\). This gives the gradient of the combined mean loss when every rank contributes the same number of equally weighted examples and computes a local mean. Unequal sample counts require matching weights, not an unqualified average of rank means.
\[
g_{\mathrm{global}} = \frac{\sum_{r=0}^{N-1} g_r}{N}
\tag{2.2}\]

Gradient synchronization example: all-reduce across four ranks
A simple four-rank collective demonstrates all-reduce arithmetic across distributed workers:

Local values: The same bucket component is 0.8, 1.2, 1.0, and 1.4 on ranks 0 through 3.
Reduction: All-reduce sums the four values to 4.4.
Average: Dividing by world size 4 produces a synchronized component value of 1.1.
Update state: Every replica receives 1.1 before applying the optimizer step. With matching starting parameters, optimizer state, and update settings, each applies the same update.
Conclusion: Distinct data shards may produce different local gradients. Synchronization supplies a common optimizer input across replicas.


The equation does not require every implementation to perform a literal gather followed by division. Ring, tree, or hierarchical collective algorithms can produce the same result with different communication schedules.
For a ring schedule, \(G\) is the complete gradient bucket size in bytes and \(N\) is the number of participating ranks. The bucket is divided into \(N\) equal chunks. A reduce-scatter phase takes \(N-1\) exchanges per rank, each sending one chunk of size \(G/N\), until every rank retains one reduced chunk. An all-gather phase takes another \(N-1\) such exchanges to distribute the reduced chunks. The expression \(B_{\mathrm{ring}}\) below counts bytes sent by one rank across both phases. It receives the same amount, so a counter adding sent and received bytes reports twice this value. Protocol overhead and unequal final chunks are excluded.
\[
B_{\mathrm{ring}} ≈ \frac{2 \cdot \left(N-1\right)}{N} \cdot G
\tag{2.3}\]

Bandwidth calculation: ring all-reduce traffic for eight ranks
Calculating communication volume through a logical ring reveals per-rank bandwidth scaling:

Gradient bucket: The synchronized bucket is 1 GB.
Rank count: Eight ranks participate.
Traffic: \(2 \times (8-1) \div 8 \times 1\ \mathrm{GB} = 1.75\ \mathrm{GB}\) sent per rank, with a further 1.75 GB received.
Interpretation: That transfer repeats for many buckets each step. Effective fabric bandwidth and overlap determine the exposed delay.
Conclusion: A compute-light model can become communication-bound even when every GPU reports activity.


The data-parallel figure shows why the update needs communication: the model is replicated, while the examples used to compute each local gradient differ. Its statement that every sample is seen exactly once assumes an evenly divisible sampler with no dropped tail. The example below uses drop_last=True, so it omits a short final tail instead of repeating padding samples.






Figure 2.3: Data parallelism replicates the model while each process consumes a sampler shard. Sample coverage depends on sampler settings. The example drops the tail rather than repeating padding samples.



The following abbreviated example uses the PyTorch 2.6 DDP API with NCCL. build_model() supplies an application-specific classifier, and dataset supplies (inputs, targets) pairs. A batch of inputs has shape \([m,d]\), containing \(m\) examples with \(d\) features. The classifier returns scores of shape \([m,c]\) for \(c\) classes. Targets have shape \([m]\) and contain integer class indices. micro_batch sets \(m\), and epochs sets the number of dataset passes. The launcher supplies rank variables, and every process needs a compatible CUDA runtime and GPU. The code changes model parameters and optimizer state but writes no checkpoint or output file.

Code example: One DDP process: device binding, data partition, gradient synchronization, and optimizer update.

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, DistributedSampler

dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")
local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)

model = DDP(build_model().cuda(local_rank), device_ids=[local_rank])
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
criterion = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset, shuffle=True, drop_last=True)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, sampler=sampler, batch_size=micro_batch)
model.train()

for epoch in range(epochs):
    sampler.set_epoch(epoch)
    for inputs, targets in loader:
        inputs = inputs.cuda(local_rank)
        targets = targets.cuda(local_rank)
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        scores = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(scores, targets)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

dist.destroy_process_group()

Code walkthrough: PyTorch DDP training step
The distributed training loop coordinates rank processes and gradient synchronization:

Process group: init_process_group joins the rank to the NCCL collective group created by the launcher.
Device assignment: LOCAL_RANK binds this process and its model replica to one GPU on the node.
Data partition: DistributedSampler gives each rank a slice, and set_epoch changes the shuffle between epochs. drop_last=True drops the tail if the dataset length does not divide evenly across ranks, avoiding duplicated padding samples.
Prediction and target: model(inputs) computes class scores. CrossEntropyLoss compares them with the integer targets and returns a scalar mean loss. AdamW retains optimizer state and updates this model’s parameters.
Synchronization point: loss.backward() activates DDP bucket hooks, and optimizer.step() consumes the reduced gradients after the required collectives finish.
Result: Every rank computes on different examples but applies the same synchronized update.
Limits: The compact loop omits mixed precision, gradient accumulation, checkpointing, validation, and worker recovery. All ranks must execute the same number of backward calls. A failed or missing rank can make peers wait until the communication timeout, after which the job controller must recover the group.

text:
2.4 Model-state sharding with ZeRO and FSDP
DDP increases throughput when one full training replica fits on each device. When persistent state or activations exceed device memory, replication is the wrong baseline. The constrained memory object determines what is sharded, and the resulting communication is placed on the available topology.
Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) removes repeated copies of training state across data-parallel processes. Its stages differ in which copies they remove. Using the 128 GB subtotal above on four ranks gives a concrete comparison. Here the optimizer-related state is the 32 GB master-weight copy plus 64 GB of Adam moment buffers, totaling 96 GB.

ZeRO-1 partitions those optimizer-related buffers. Each rank updates only its assigned parameters, and the updated values are shared so all ranks retain a complete low-precision model. The per-rank subtotal becomes \(16 + 16 + 96/4 = 56\) GB: full weights, full gradients, and one optimizer shard.
ZeRO-2 also partitions reduced gradients. A reduce-scatter leaves each rank with the gradients needed for its optimizer shard. Updated parameter shards are then exchanged to restore each full weight replica. The subtotal becomes \(16 + 16/4 + 96/4 = 44\) GB.
ZeRO-3 also partitions the low-precision parameters. Each rank gathers the parameters needed for the current layer during forward and backward execution, then releases those full copies according to its reuse policy. The subtotal becomes \((16 + 16 + 96)/4 = 32\) GB before these temporary gathers.

The stage definitions follow DeepSpeed’s ZeRO description. The arithmetic applies the same illustrative precision policy to each stage. It is not a peak-memory prediction: activations, bucket buffers, temporary parameters, and allocator reserve still have to fit. If 56 GB plus that working memory fits, ZeRO-1 may be sufficient. If gradients still prevent the run from fitting, ZeRO-2 removes their replicated storage. ZeRO-3 is useful when complete weight replicas are themselves too costly, at the expense of repeated parameter gathers.
Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) is PyTorch’s implementation family for sharded data parallelism. Its full-sharding mode shares the main state-placement pattern of ZeRO-3, but the APIs, wrapping units, precision settings, and checkpoint formats are not interchangeable. Neither method alone removes activation memory. Saving fewer activations and recomputing them during backward execution, called activation checkpointing, exchanges additional computation for a smaller \(A\) term.
Other strategies address different memory and sequence constraints:

Tensor parallelism: splits matrix operations across devices and communicates partial results within each layer.
Pipeline parallelism: places consecutive layer groups on stages and streams micro-batches through them.
Sequence or context parallelism: splits token-dependent state and computation for long sequences.
Expert parallelism: places Mixture-of-Experts sub-networks on different devices and routes tokens to their selected experts.

FSDP reduces replicated state but increases parameter communication. Tensor parallelism reduces per-device matrix state but adds frequent collective operations. Pipeline parallelism reduces layer residency but creates bubbles when stages wait. Context and expert parallelism add workload-specific routing and balance problems. Large runs combine strategies only after measuring the simpler baseline.

State sharding comparison: FSDP memory savings versus full replication
Sharding model states across ranks reduces per-GPU memory footprints in exchange for collective communication:

Replicated baseline: Four DDP ranks each hold the complete 128 GB model-state subtotal from the 8B Adam example.
Ideal four-way shard: Sharding parameters, gradients, master weights, and optimizer buffers divides that subtotal to about 32 GB per rank before temporary gathers and activations.
Execution trace: Before one layer executes, each rank gathers the required parameter shards. After backward computation, reduce-scatter leaves each rank with its gradient shard.
New constraint: Temporary all-gathers, activation memory, allocator reserve, and communication overlap still determine whether the run fits and performs well.
Conclusion: Sharding changes where state resides. The saved copies are exchanged for temporary buffers and communication.


The hybrid-parallelism figure connects these choices to the physical links: frequent exchanges benefit most from nearby devices, while broader groups use the inter-node fabric.

text:
2.5 Coordinating workers through rendezvous
A selected strategy describes state placement. Processes still need unique identities and a common group before they can exchange any tensor. Ranks and rendezvous form the process group before the communication backend carries collective traffic.

Rank: The unique integer identity of one process inside a distributed process group.
World size: The total number of participating processes in that group.
Local rank: The process index within one node, commonly used to select the local GPU.
Rendezvous: The control-plane handshake through which processes discover one another, agree on membership, and obtain group metadata.

torchrun starts processes and supplies LOCAL_RANK, RANK, and WORLD_SIZE. A store reachable through MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT coordinates rendezvous. In this example, NCCL is the selected collective backend and establishes the GPU data paths after init_process_group completes. Other hardware and execution environments can use other compatible backends. The rendezvous store is not the channel carrying each gradient. The process-identity figure distinguishes global identities from the local indices used to select devices.






Figure 2.5: Global rank, node rank, and local rank identify every distributed process.



This abbreviated POSIX shell command uses the PyTorch 2.6 torchrun launcher. It runs once on each of two allocated nodes. NODE_RANK is 0 on the first node and 1 on the second, and MASTER_ADDR is the reachable address of the first node. Both nodes need the same train.py, environment, and eight visible GPUs. The command starts processes and can run a training job when those application inputs exist. It contains no provisioning or recovery policy.

Code example: Two-node torchrun launch definition for sixteen training processes.


torchrun \
  --nnodes=2 \
  --nproc-per-node=8 \
  --node-rank="${NODE_RANK}" \
  --master-addr="${MASTER_ADDR}" \
  --master-port=29500 \
  train.py

Code walkthrough: multi-node torchrun invocation
The launcher CLI coordinates cluster rendezvous and process rank binding:

Cluster shape: --nnodes=2 and --nproc-per-node=8 declare sixteen expected processes.
Node identity: --node-rank gives each launcher a unique identity within the rendezvous.
Rendezvous endpoint: The master address and port identify the shared control endpoint used to form the process group.
Injected state: torchrun supplies global rank, local rank, and world size to each train.py process.
Result: The launcher describes membership. The training program still initializes the process group and binds each local rank to a GPU.
Limits: Both nodes share rendezvous settings, reachable networking, matching code and environment, and a scheduler allocation that starts the full group.



Rendezvous diagnosis: root causes of distributed hangs
Process synchronization failures during initialization often appear as unresponsive jobs:

A wrong rank count, unreachable master address, blocked port, or partially scheduled job often looks like a hang because processes wait for missing peers.
Process identities and control-plane connectivity are the first checks because either can create a hang before NCCL bandwidth becomes relevant.

2.6 Workload scheduling on GPU clusters
Rendezvous requires every expected rank to appear. A cluster scheduler that starts only part of a multi-node job can consume GPUs while making no progress. A complete scheduling setup exposes devices, admits the full worker group together, and isolates resources.
A GPU becomes available to Kubernetes only after the host driver, container runtime integration, and NVIDIA device plugin or GPU Operator expose nvidia.com/gpu. A pod requests an integer device count. Labels and node affinity select the GPU family, while taints restrict which workloads may use expensive GPU nodes. A toleration permits placement on a tainted node but does not itself select that node. The figure separates device availability from placement rules.






Figure 2.6: Kubernetes exposes GPUs as schedulable resources and uses labels, taints, and tolerations to place workloads.



The following abbreviated Kubernetes batch/v1 Job and core v1 Pod specification request two workers with eight GPUs each. The image digest is a placeholder, so the manifest is not ready to submit. It describes resources and allowed node placement, not a complete distributed launch. A controller must still assign worker identities and arrange the torchrun environment. Neither this object nor its parallelism field guarantees that both pods start together.

Code example: Kubernetes GPU resource declaration for two distributed worker pods.


apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: ddp-worker
spec:
  completions: 2
  parallelism: 2
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      tolerations:
        - key: nvidia.com/gpu
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
      affinity:
        nodeAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            nodeSelectorTerms:
              - matchExpressions:
                  - key: accelerator.fabric
                    operator: In
                    values: [nvlink]
      containers:
        - name: trainer
          image: registry.example/trainer@sha256:...
          resources:
            requests:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 8
            limits:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 8

Code walkthrough: Kubernetes distributed worker manifest
The declarative pod specification defines resource allocation and cluster scheduling:

Replica state: completions and parallelism request two worker pods, but the base Job object does not give them distributed rank identities.
GPU admission: Matching request and limit values reserve eight whole GPUs for each worker.
Placement permission: The toleration allows the worker onto nodes protected by the GPU taint. Required node affinity also selects nodes labeled accelerator.fabric=nvlink.
Artifact identity: The image digest makes both workers execute the same immutable training environment.
Result: The manifest requests sixteen GPUs across two pods. Additional scheduler and launcher integration is needed for group admission and rendezvous.
Limits: A complete deployment also needs worker indexing, service discovery, volumes, security context, retry policy, and a distributed-job controller or scheduler integration.



Gang scheduling: An all-or-nothing allocation policy that starts a distributed job only when its complete resource set is available.

This abbreviated Volcano scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 PodGroup declares a minimum group size of two pods and sixteen GPUs. That is a scheduler API version, not a tested cluster installation. The Volcano scheduler and matching custom resource definition must be installed. Creating the PodGroup alone does not associate it with the preceding Job.

Code example: A gang-admission object declares that both workers and all sixteen GPUs form one scheduling unit.


apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: ddp-two-node
spec:
  minMember: 2
  minResources:
    nvidia.com/gpu: "16"

Code walkthrough: admission requirements for a worker group

Group identity: metadata.name identifies ddp-two-node, which the worker pods must reference through the configured Volcano integration.
Pod count: minMember: 2 requires two members before the minimum group can be admitted.
GPU count: minResources requires sixteen GPUs for that group, while individual pod requests determine how they must fit onto nodes.
Missing association: The earlier Job does not select the Volcano scheduler or identify this group. A complete integration sets schedulerName: volcano and the supported pod-to-group association, or uses a Volcano Job controller to create and connect its worker group.
Result and limits: An integrated group can wait without admitting only its minimum subset. It can remain pending indefinitely when the required resources never become available. Gang admission does not repair a process crash after startup or replace rank assignment, launch timeouts, and checkpoint recovery.


The Volcano PodGroup documentation defines these admission fields. The figure shows the scheduling problem they address: partially allocated workers cannot complete a collective that expects absent peers. Its simultaneous-start wording means all-or-none admission. Process launch and readiness can still finish at different times.






Figure 2.7: Gang admission prevents a job from holding only part of its requested GPU set. Admission does not make every process ready at exactly the same time.



Volcano provides gang scheduling for tightly coupled jobs, while Kueue adds queue and quota management around the default Kubernetes scheduler. SkyPilot abstracts resource provisioning across clouds and clusters. Slurm provides queueing and accounting. Soperator runs the Slurm control plane on Kubernetes so Slurm manages jobs while Kubernetes manages pods and nodes.

2.7 Recovering distributed jobs from checkpoints
Gang admission makes the full worker allocation available. Process startup and readiness still require coordination. At cluster scale, hardware, network, process, and preemptible-capacity failures make a long uninterrupted run unlikely. The acceptable progress loss and recovery time determine checkpoint frequency, layout, and persistence.

Recovery Point Objective (RPO): The maximum amount of completed training progress the system may lose after a failure.
Recovery Time Objective (RTO): The maximum acceptable time between failure and resumed useful training.

A resumable checkpoint includes model parameters, optimizer state, scheduler state, step or epoch, random-number-generator state, and data-loader position when exact sample order matters. DDP may let rank 0 save the unwrapped model, while sharded strategies require a compatible distributed-checkpoint format. The recovery figure connects these saved objects to checkpoint frequency and the path into durable storage. Its intervals and cost figures are examples, not defaults. Its same-topology statement applies to formats that cannot reshard at load time. PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint can save under one cluster topology and load under another.






Figure 2.8: Recovery objectives shape checkpoint frequency and persistence. The displayed intervals and costs are examples. Topology requirements depend on checkpoint format and resharding support.



A fast path copies a consistent snapshot into host memory or local NVMe, returns GPU control quickly, and copies asynchronously to shared or object storage. Local state may survive a process failure, but it does not cover loss of that node. Node-loss recovery is covered only after the background copy completes. Section 5.3 develops the storage-to-GPU input path, including when direct transfer can help. It is distinct from deciding when a checkpoint is safe to restore.
A checkpoint becomes restorable through an ordered publication path:

Write a temporary generation. Every rank writes its shard under a generation-specific temporary prefix. The live restore pointer remains unchanged.
Verify the generation. The coordinator checks the expected shard count, file hashes, training step, model configuration, and writer completion from every rank.
Publish the commit record. A small manifest names the verified shards and compatibility metadata. Readers discover the generation only after this record is complete. A separate current-generation pointer, if used, needs the selected storage service’s single-object atomic or conditional-update guarantee. This does not make all shard writes one atomic transaction.
Validate restore. A test reader reconstructs model, optimizer, scheduler, random state, and data position before the generation enters the recovery set.
Ignore incomplete state. A missing shard or absent commit record leaves the previous committed generation as the restore target.


Checkpoint interval satisfying an average-loss target
An average-loss target gives an interval bound under a stated failure model:

Illustrative run cost: A 64-GPU job at an assumed $180 per GPU-hour costs $11,520 per wall-clock hour. These values illustrate the calculation, not a quoted service price.
Allowed average lost work: The team accepts at most 15 minutes on average.
Periodic-failure assumption: A failure is equally likely within one checkpoint interval, so average lost work is approximately half the interval.
Interval: To keep the average at 15 minutes, checkpoint every 30 minutes.
I/O check: If checkpoint starts are 30 wall-clock minutes apart and each pauses the GPUs for 4 minutes, checkpointing occupies \(4/30\), or 13.3%, of that time. If the interval instead means 30 minutes of useful training plus a 4-minute pause, the fraction is \(4/34\), or 11.8%.
Conclusion: This is an interval satisfying the illustrative average-loss target, not a cost optimum. Asynchronous persistence may reduce the pause, but its completion delay can leave more progress exposed to node failure.


The half-interval average assumes failures are uniformly distributed over useful progress between completed durable checkpoints. A maximum-loss RPO requires a separate bound on the oldest recoverable state, including write and copy delays. Finding an economic optimum would also require failure frequency, checkpoint cost, and recovery time. The example does not supply those inputs.

2.8 Measuring scaling efficiency and diagnosing stragglers
A recoverable job can survive expected failure. It may still waste accelerators through data starvation, synchronization, pipeline bubbles, or unstable numerics. Useful-work measurements and training, GPU, and communication evidence localize the delay.
Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) compares the rate of useful model arithmetic with the hardware’s corresponding peak. \(F_{\mathrm{observed}}\) is estimated model floating-point operations per token multiplied by measured tokens per second. \(F_{\mathrm{peak}}\) is the combined peak floating-point operations per second for all participating devices at the precision used. Their ratio is informative only when precision, device count, and arithmetic conventions match. Extra work such as activation recomputation may consume hardware time without counting as useful model arithmetic in the numerator.
\[
\mathrm{MFU} = \frac{F_{\mathrm{observed}}}{F_{\mathrm{peak}}}
\tag{2.4}\]

MFU calculation: Model FLOPs Utilization for an eight-GPU cluster
Comparing observed floating-point throughput against hardware peak quantifies compute efficiency:

Observed work per token: For an illustrative model and training objective, the arithmetic estimate is 120 GFLOPs per processed token.
Measured throughput: The eight-GPU run processes 20,000 tokens each second.
Observed rate: 20,000 tokens/s × 120 GFLOPs/token = 2.4 PFLOPs/s of model arithmetic.
Relevant peak: Eight devices provide a combined 8.0 PFLOPs/s peak at the precision used by the run.
Utilization: Dividing 2.4 by 8.0 gives 0.30, or 30% MFU.
Diagnosis: The remaining 70% may come from input wait, memory traffic, kernels, collectives, imbalance, or bubbles. It is not automatically communication loss.
Conclusion: MFU quantifies the gap, while correlated timelines and counters identify where the lost time originates.


GPU utilization alone can be misleading because a device may report activity while waiting on memory or communication. Throughput, MFU, power draw, memory-bandwidth utilization, NVLink or InfiniBand traffic, step-time variance, and collective traces provide the comparison. A straggler slows every synchronized rank.

Timeline diagnosis: identifying straggler ranks
Analyzing per-rank execution phases exposes load imbalance across cluster workers:

Ranks 0–6 finish input loading in 45 ms, while rank 7 takes 130 ms. All ranks then participate in the same collective, whose useful transfer takes 70 ms after the last rank arrives.
The collective appears long on every timeline because seven ranks wait for rank 7 before useful transfer can complete. The unequal pre-collective gap identifies input or host work on rank 7 as the first cause to investigate.


The efficiency figure brings training progress, device activity, recovery, and cost into the same measurement view. No single utilization counter establishes that the run is efficient. The formula reference links back to the memory, communication, and MFU calculations.






Figure 2.9: Training efficiency combines throughput, utilization, recovery, and cost rather than one GPU-utilization number.

text:
3.1 Setting latency and throughput targets
How does a versioned model become a responsive, efficient, and reversible user-facing service? Chapter 2 treated one coordinated training job whose ranks progress together. Serving replaces synchronized steps with variable-length requests, latency objectives, retained KV-cache state, and rolling changes across a fleet.
The service must respond quickly without admitting more work than its memory and compute can carry. The map follows a request through routing and execution, then connects its working memory to capacity and release decisions. These controls use the same fixed model parameters, but change when and where the service processes each request.
A checkpoint is only one ingredient of a user-facing release. The serving design cannot be optimized until success is stated in workload and business terms. Latency, throughput, memory, quality, and cost measurements give engine settings a clear objective.
Language-model inference has two phases. Prefill processes the prompt tokens and prepares attention state. Decode then generates successive output tokens, each conditioned on the earlier tokens. The key-value (KV) cache retains the key and value tensors used by attention so the engine can reuse earlier token state during decode. It is working memory for a request, not a change to the model parameters. A token is an entry in the model’s tokenizer vocabulary and may represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment. Section 3.3 follows actual request text into that representation.
The business objective combines accepted work per GPU with latency, quality, safety, and availability. A benchmark that doubles tokens/s but violates the user’s ITL target does not improve that service.
Let \(N_{\mathrm{out}}\) be the number of generated output tokens, with at least one token. TTFT already includes the first token, leaving \(N_{\mathrm{out}}-1\) later intervals. Multiplying their mean ITL by that count and adding TTFT gives the approximate total request time \(T_{\mathrm{request}}\). Every time term must use the same unit, such as milliseconds. For one fully observed request, summing its actual intervals is exact. The approximation is useful for planning with an estimated mean interval, but combining unrelated percentile measurements does not produce a valid total-latency percentile.
\[
T_{\mathrm{request}} ≈ \mathrm{TTFT} + \left(N_{\mathrm{out}}-1\right) \cdot \mathrm{ITL}
\tag{3.1}\]
The batch-size figure relates these latency measurements to throughput. A wider batch is useful only within the service’s response-time limits.
Latency distributions reveal behavior that a mean can hide. The p95 or p99 TTFT exposes queue spikes and long prompts, while ITL exposes decode instability. A complete throughput measurement states prompt and output lengths, concurrency pattern, engine configuration, GPU type, quantization, and whether routing and gateway overhead are included.

text:
Service Level Objective (SLO): A measurable target for service behavior over a stated window. A p95 time-to-first-token below a threshold is one example.
Time to First Token (TTFT): Elapsed time from request admission until the first generated token becomes available.
Inter-Token Latency (ITL): Time between successive generated tokens during decode, commonly summarized as a distribution.
Throughput: Completed useful work per unit time, such as output tokens per second per GPU or requests per second at a defined workload.





Latency breakdown: prefill and decode phases for interactive serving
Measuring request latency components separates prompt processing from token generation:

Queue: The request waits 120 ms.
Prefill and first-token work: Processing a 2,000-token prompt and making the first token available takes 280 ms after queueing.
First token: The measured TTFT is 120 + 280 = 400 ms within this request-admission boundary.
Later tokens: The remaining 79 intervals average 22 ms, adding 1,738 ms.
Total: 400 + 79 × 22 = 2,138 ms.
Interpretation: Later-token decode dominates total time even though the first-token experience remains separately visible.
Conclusion: A single latency number hides the stage that limits the request.

3.2 Routing a request through the serving system
The serving objective identifies what users and operators measure. Those measurements cross several components, and each component owns a different decision. One request passes through admission, routing, and execution, while fleet management and evidence collection run around that data path.
The request path separates five concrete responsibilities:

API gateway: authenticates identities, validates request shape, enforces quotas and rate limits, applies policy filters, and records billing identity.
Inference router: selects an eligible engine replica using health, queue, model placement, and cache-state evidence.
Inference engine: tokenizes, schedules batches, allocates KV-cache blocks, executes kernels, and streams generated tokens.
Control plane: reconciles desired model deployments, provisions capacity, distributes weights, rolls versions, and coordinates recovery.
Data and observability layer: stores request traces, metrics, logs, audit events, evaluation samples, and release evidence.

The architecture figure places the gateway, router, and engine on the request path, with fleet control and durable records around it.






Figure 3.3: A production LLM request crosses gateway, router, engine, control-plane, and observability responsibilities.



The router lies on the live request path, while the control plane normally does not. Healthy replicas can continue serving during a temporary control-plane outage. A router without fresh health or queue state can still send traffic to an overloaded or corrupt engine, even when provisioning is healthy.

Request trace: lifecycle state transitions
Tracking request state transitions exposes lifecycle delays through the serving engine:

The gateway accepts request req-1842 for serving bundle sb-27 and records tenant and quota state. The router sees replicas A and B as compatible, but A’s health record is older than the 10-second freshness limit.
Replica A is excluded. Replica B receives the request, allocates KV blocks, streams tokens, and emits completion state. If every compatible health record is stale, the router returns a bounded unavailable response instead of guessing that an endpoint is healthy.

title: 3  Serving LLMs with predictable performance
text:
3.3 Separating prefill and decode latency
The request path identifies the engine as the component that turns admitted text into tokens. Inside the engine, queueing, prompt processing, and token generation stress different resources. The normal request path provides the baseline for stage-specific controls.
Text arrives as strings of unequal length, but the GPU performs numerical operations on arrays. A tokenizer fixed by the serving bundle maps each string into an ordered list of integer token IDs. The model’s embedding lookup converts each ID to a vector of a fixed width. Position information records where each token occurs. This conversion lets the model apply shared matrix operations, but tokenization choices affect sequence length, memory, and compatibility with the trained weights.
Consider two requests, A containing Can I return this? and B containing Refund status?. For a simplified tokenizer, A becomes [11, 24, 31, 42, 7] and B becomes [58, 62, 7]. These invented IDs illustrate the mapping, not a particular production vocabulary. A padded implementation could create a two-row, five-column ID array by extending B to [58, 62, 7, 0, 0]. Lengths [5, 3] and a padding mask distinguish real tokens from placeholders. A causal attention mask also prevents an earlier position from using future token content. Selecting the last real prompt position for each request produces its next-token prediction without treating padding as input text.
The rectangular batch supports shared execution, but two of its ten slots contain no useful prompt token. Some serving engines pack only real tokens and use sequence offsets, lengths, and block tables instead of this rectangular padded layout. Both approaches must preserve request identity and token order. Packing reduces unused work but requires kernels and scheduling that interpret the extra control data. After the first generated token, each active sequence contributes its next decode position, while its prior tokens remain represented in the KV cache. Section 3.5 explains how that growing state maps to physical memory.

Prefill: The parallel forward pass over prompt tokens that computes hidden states and initializes key/value tensors for attention.
Decode: The autoregressive loop that produces one next token per sequence iteration while reading accumulated KV-cache state.

Prefill performs large matrix operations over many prompt tokens and is commonly compute-bound. Decode repeatedly streams model weights and KV state for a small amount of arithmetic per active sequence, so memory bandwidth and batch width often dominate. Queueing is controlled by admission and scheduler policy rather than a GPU kernel.






Figure 3.4: Latency controls act separately on queueing, prompt prefill, token decode, and cross-stage execution.



A useful latency diagnosis identifies the stage. Long queue delay suggests admission, capacity, or scheduling pressure. Long prefill suggests very long prompts, poor prefix reuse, or insufficient prefill compute. High ITL suggests decode batching, memory bandwidth, cache pressure, or per-token synchronization.

Workload comparison: short-context versus long-context serving dynamics
Varying prompt and generation token counts shifts the bottleneck between compute and memory bandwidth:

Long prompt: A 12,000-token prompt spends 1,450 ms in prefill and then emits 20 tokens at 18 ms between tokens.
Long answer: A 600-token prompt spends 110 ms in prefill and then emits 180 tokens at 24 ms between tokens.
Comparison: The first request is prefill-dominated. The second is decode-dominated even though its prompt is much smaller.
Control choice: Prefix reuse or more prefill capacity helps the first shape, while decode batch width and KV pressure are more relevant to the second.
Conclusion: Prompt and output distributions select the useful optimization. Request count alone does not.

text:
3.4 Increasing throughput with continuous batching
The request stages have distinct costs, while static batches force short sequences to wait for the longest member and leave holes after requests finish. Continuous batching recovers those slots through iteration-level admission and completion.

Continuous batching: A serving scheduler that adds waiting sequences and removes finished sequences between decode iterations.

The scheduler has a token budget, not merely a request-count limit. It chooses a mix of new prefill tokens and active decode tokens for the next iteration. Wider batches increase throughput by reusing weight reads across sequences, but they also increase queue time and can degrade ITL if the GPU is oversubscribed.

Chunked prefill: Splitting a long prompt into smaller prefill chunks so decode work from other requests can be interleaved.

Chunked prefill protects interactive decode traffic from a single very long prompt. The trade-off is more scheduling overhead and potentially less efficient prompt computation. Its production behavior depends on the actual mix of prompt sizes and latency classes.

Continuous batching: purpose and limits
Continuous batching balances useful execution against queue delay and per-token latency:

Works on: The serving-engine queue and active sequence set.
Helps when: Requests have different arrival times and output lengths.
How it works: Rebuilds the batch between iterations so completed sequences leave and waiting sequences enter.
Other limits: Larger batches improve throughput but can increase queue delay and per-token latency.
Why it matters: It prevents variable-length traffic from wasting GPU slots behind finished or unusually long requests.


The scheduling figure shows the active batch changing as sequences finish. The important boundary is an iteration: a waiting request can enter without waiting for every earlier request to complete.






Figure 3.5: Iteration-level scheduling admits and removes sequences as their prompt and decode work changes.




Batch iteration trace: continuous batching sequence
Observing token generation across consecutive iterations reveals batching behavior that changes over time:

Iteration 1 admits requests A and B for prefill. Iteration 2 decodes A and B while request C waits because the token budget is full.
B finishes after iteration 2. Iteration 3 removes B, admits C’s prefill chunk, and continues A’s decode. The active set changes without waiting for A to finish.
The expected effect is fewer empty execution slots. The measured limits are queue delay and ITL for each latency class.


The following abbreviated Python configuration uses settings documented for vLLM 0.8.5. Evaluating the dictionary creates engine_args but starts no engine and processes no request. An application would supply a model identity and pass these values to the matching engine constructor. The values are illustrative, not measured capacity settings. Unsupported configurations or insufficient memory can prevent engine startup, and this block contains no exception handling or retry policy.

Code example: vLLM 0.8.5 scheduler and cache-capacity settings, without engine startup.


# Abbreviated configuration for vLLM 0.8.5.
engine_args = {
    "max_num_seqs": 128,
    "max_num_batched_tokens": 8192,
    "enable_chunked_prefill": True,
    "gpu_memory_utilization": 0.90,
}

Code walkthrough: scheduler and memory limits
These settings constrain the work that the engine can admit:

Sequence ceiling: max_num_seqs bounds the number of active request sequences considered by the scheduler.
Token budget: max_num_batched_tokens caps prompt and decode tokens admitted to one iteration’s work.
Prefill policy: enable_chunked_prefill permits long prompts to be split so interactive decode work can interleave.
Memory reserve: gpu_memory_utilization controls how much device memory the engine may use for weights, KV blocks, and execution buffers.
Result: The settings jointly affect admission, batch shape, queueing behavior, and KV-cache capacity. Raising the sequence ceiling cannot create cache space beyond the memory budget.
Limits: The vLLM 0.8.5 engine arguments define these options. Other versions and engines can impose different scheduling rules. A configuration dictionary does not show the scheduler’s implementation or establish its performance.
